tagline: How a holy God can live among an unholy people: sacrifice, priesthood, purity, and a whole life set apart for him and for the neighbor.
overview:
Leviticus begins at the exact moment Exodus ends. The tabernacle has been set up, the cloud of God's glory has filled it, and Moses cannot go in. The book's first line answers that problem: the LORD calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and begins to explain how people may come near. What follows is the Bible's fullest account of sacrifice, priesthood, ritual purity, sacred time, and holiness in daily life. There are five kinds of offering, the ordination of Aaron and his sons, laws about food, childbirth, skin disease, and bodily discharges, the yearly Day of Atonement, and a long call to holiness that reaches into farming, business, sex, the courts, and the treatment of immigrants and the poor.

Many readers stall here, because the detail is dense and the world is unfamiliar. But Leviticus is answering one of the Bible's central questions: how can a holy God dwell in the middle of a people who are not holy without destroying them? Its answer is not that sin and death don't matter. It is that God himself provides a way, through blood, priesthood, washing, and an ordered common life, for a forgiven people to live near him. The book's most famous command, “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (19:2), stands only a few verses from its other famous line, “love your neighbor as yourself” (19:18). Leviticus will not separate worship from ethics.

For Christians it is the dictionary behind the New Testament's language about Jesus: sacrifice, atonement, high priest, clean and unclean, the veil, the blood. The Letter to the Hebrews can hardly be read without it. In Judaism, after the temple and its sacrifices ended in AD 70, the book remained central, reread through prayer, study, and deeds of kindness, and its food and purity laws continue to shape Jewish life.
author:
Leviticus names no author, but it presents nearly everything in it as speech from the LORD to Moses, sometimes to Moses and Aaron together, at Mount Sinai (1:1; 26:46; 27:34). Jewish and Christian tradition has accordingly counted it among the five books of Moses, and in the Gospels Jesus sends a healed leper to offer what Moses commanded for his cleansing (Mark 1:44), referring to the law of Leviticus 14 as Moses' law. Many conservative scholars, Gordon Wenham among them in his 1979 commentary, argue that the book's substance goes back to Moses and the wilderness period, whatever later editing it received.

Since the nineteenth century most critical scholars have assigned Leviticus to the Priestly source, one of the strands the documentary hypothesis finds woven through the first five books, and have treated chapters 17 to 26 as a distinct collection called the Holiness Code, named for its refrain about being holy as the LORD is holy. Opinion within that approach has shifted. Older critics thought the Holiness Code was earlier and was absorbed by the Priestly writers; Jacob Milgrom and Israel Knohl argued the reverse, that a later Holiness school edited and extended the Priestly material. Readers across these views agree that the book preserves the ritual knowledge of Israel's priesthood, knowledge that priestly families guarded and handed down with great care.
date:
The date follows the authorship question. Read as Mosaic, the book comes from the wilderness period just after the exodus, which is itself dated in two main ways: about 1446 BC, from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1, or in the thirteenth century BC, often linked with the store city Rameses named in Exodus 1:11.

Julius Wellhausen's influential reconstruction in the late nineteenth century placed the Priestly writing in or after the Babylonian exile, in the sixth or fifth century BC, as the charter of the rebuilt temple community. Other scholars, including Yehezkel Kaufmann and Jacob Milgrom, argued that the priestly laws are largely earlier than the exile, pointing to linguistic studies that find their Hebrew older than the language of Ezekiel, and to the fact that the laws assume a wilderness camp and a portable tent rather than the Jerusalem temple. Even a late written form can preserve far older ritual practice. Within the story itself the time covered is short: the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year after the exodus (Exodus 40:17), and Numbers opens on the first day of the second month (Numbers 1:1), so Leviticus fills about one month at Sinai.
setting:
The whole book is set at Mount Sinai, in the wilderness south of Canaan (the mountain's exact location is debated), where Israel camped for about a year after leaving Egypt. The people have received the covenant (Exodus 19 to 24), broken it with the golden calf (Exodus 32), been restored (Exodus 34), and built the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary with a courtyard, a bronze altar, and an inner room holding the ark. Leviticus pictures a camp arranged around that tent, with priests from Aaron's family serving at its altar.

Israel's neighbors all offered sacrifices, kept priesthoods, and practiced purification. Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast, from the late second millennium BC, name offerings with terms close to the Hebrew ones, and Hittite ritual texts describe driving away an animal to carry off plague or impurity, rites often compared with the scapegoat of Leviticus 16. Egyptian temples served the statues of their gods with daily meals and washings. Leviticus shares the vocabulary of that world but reshapes it. There is no image of God, and although the old language of offerings as God's food survives (3:11; 21:6), nothing in the book suggests that God needs feeding. The laws come as the words of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. The book also names practices Israel must refuse, among them child sacrifice to Molech (18:21; 20:2-5) and consulting mediums (19:31).
purpose:
Leviticus was written to teach Israel how to live with God in their midst. Its first audience was the priests, who had to know the procedures, and early Jewish tradition called the book the instruction of the priests (Torat Kohanim). Yet most of it is addressed to the whole people. Chapter after chapter opens with the charge, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them”, and the priests' own task is to “distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean” and to teach Israel accordingly (10:10-11). The goal of it all is stated in the covenant promise near the end: “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (26:12).

For later readers the book did more. Its warnings that the land would vomit out a people who defiled it (18:28; 20:22) explained the exile to those who lived through it, and its promise that God would remember his covenant even in the land of their enemies (26:44-45) gave them ground to hope.
story:
Leviticus is the middle book of the five books of Moses and the hinge between Exodus and Numbers. Genesis tells how humanity was driven from God's presence in Eden. Exodus tells how God rescued Israel from Egypt and came to dwell among them in the tabernacle. Leviticus explains how that dwelling can last. Numbers then takes the ordered camp out into the wilderness toward Canaan, and Deuteronomy restates the law on the edge of the land.

The book's patterns run through the rest of Scripture. The temple of Solomon carries on the tabernacle's worship. The prophets condemn sacrifice offered without justice (Isaiah 1; Amos 5), not because Leviticus was wrong but because Israel had split what it joined. Ezekiel, a priest, draws heavily on the book's language in his indictments and his vision of a new temple. And the Day of Atonement, the scapegoat, the Jubilee, and the call to holiness all return in the New Testament.
christ:
The New Testament reads Leviticus in the light of Jesus more closely than almost any other Old Testament book. Hebrews argues that Christ is the great high priest who entered not a sanctuary made with hands but heaven itself, with his own blood, once for all (Hebrews 9:11-14, 24-28), and that the Day of Atonement's yearly repetition showed that animal blood could not finally take away sins (Hebrews 10:1-4). Paul says God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice, using the Greek word that the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses for the mercy seat on the ark (Romans 3:25). Hebrews 13:11-12 compares the sin offering burned outside the camp with Jesus suffering outside the city gate.

In the Gospels Jesus touches the unclean, a leper and a woman with a long flow of blood, and instead of contracting their impurity he makes them clean (Mark 1:40-45; 5:25-34), while still sending the healed man to the priest with the offering Leviticus required. He names “love your neighbor as yourself” as the second great commandment (Mark 12:31), and 1 Peter 1:16 repeats the call to be holy as God is holy. The church has read all this as fulfillment rather than cancellation. The sacrifices and purity laws pointed toward a cleansing and nearness that Christ provides, which is why Christians do not offer animals and why most do not keep the food laws (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
reading:
Leviticus is mostly instruction: ritual procedures, case laws (if a person does this, then that), and lists, broken by two short narratives (chapters 8 to 10 and 24:10-23). Read it as you would the working rules of a sacred house, asking what each rule assumes about God, sin, life, and death.

Three misreadings are common. The first is that Israel earned God's favor by sacrifice; but the book is given to a people already rescued from Egypt (11:45; 26:13), and sacrifice is God's provision for keeping that relationship whole. The second is that unclean means sinful. Much impurity came from ordinary and even good things, such as childbirth, burying the dead, or a normal bodily discharge, and it was removed by time and washing; sin and impurity overlap but are not the same. The third is treating the laws as random taboos. Scholars have offered several explanations: the anthropologist Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), argued that clean animals are those that fit their category completely, so the laws teach wholeness; Jacob Milgrom argued that impurity is bound up with death and the laws train Israel to choose life; others stress separation from the practices of Canaan, or health.

Christians also differ on how the law applies now. A long tradition, found in Thomas Aquinas and in the Reformation confessions, distinguishes moral, ceremonial, and civil laws and holds that only the moral law binds believers directly. Others read the whole law as fulfilled in Christ and brought to believers through his teaching. Both take Leviticus as Christian Scripture.

structure.title: The offerings
structure.summary: Five kinds of offering (burnt, grain, peace, sin or purification, and guilt or reparation), first described from the worshiper's side and then as instructions for the priests who handle them.

structure.title: The priests ordained
structure.summary: Moses ordains Aaron and his sons over seven days. On the eighth day God's glory appears and fire consumes the offering, and then Nadab and Abihu die for offering unauthorized fire.

structure.title: Clean and unclean
structure.summary: Laws on food, childbirth, skin diseases and mold, and bodily discharges, with the rites that restore an unclean person to the community and the sanctuary.

structure.title: The Day of Atonement
structure.summary: Once a year the high priest enters the Most Holy Place to cleanse the sanctuary of Israel's impurities, and a live goat carries the people's sins away into the wilderness.

structure.title: Holiness in all of life
structure.summary: The Holiness Code: blood, sexual relations, love of neighbor, penalties, the holiness of priests and offerings, the yearly feasts, the Sabbath year and Jubilee, and the covenant's blessings and curses.

structure.title: Vows and dedications
structure.summary: Rules for dedicating people, animals, houses, and fields to the LORD, for redeeming them, and for the tithe, closing the book with a note that these commands were given at Sinai.

themes.title: Holiness
themes.body: The Hebrew word qadosh, holy, marks what belongs to God and is set apart from common use. God is holy in his otherness and his moral purity, and his holiness spreads outward from the Most Holy Place to the priests, the people, their calendar, and their land. The refrain “be holy, because I am holy” (11:44) is not a call to religious performance but to a whole life that matches the God who lives among them.

themes.title: God's presence among his people
themes.body: Everything in the book assumes that God actually lives in the middle of the camp. That is Israel's greatest gift and its greatest danger, as the deaths of Nadab and Abihu show (chapter 10). The laws exist so that the presence can stay, and the book's high point is the promise that God will make his dwelling among them and walk among them (26:11-12).

themes.title: Atonement and sacrifice
themes.body: The verb kipper, to make atonement, runs through the book. Sacrifice is more than dealing with sin: there are gifts, thanksgiving, and shared meals as well as purification and reparation. But at its center is the conviction that sin and impurity are deadly, and that God gives the blood of a substitute to cover them: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood” (17:11).

themes.title: Clean and unclean
themes.body: Impurity is a state, not always a sin. It comes from contact with death, disease, and the loss of life-fluids, and it bars a person from the sanctuary until time, washing, and sometimes an offering restore them. The system taught Israel, daily and physically, that the God of life cannot be approached casually by creatures touched by death.

themes.title: Justice, land, and neighbor
themes.body: Holiness in Leviticus is social. Farmers leave the edges of their fields for the poor and the foreigner, wages are paid the same day, the deaf and blind are protected, the foreigner is loved as oneself (19:34), and every fiftieth year land returns to its families, because “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine” (25:23).

keyChapters.why: The burnt offering, the whole gift wholly given, opens the book and introduces the laying on of hands and the language of atonement.
Nadab and Abihu die before the LORD, a stark lesson that nearness to a holy God is a gift that cannot be handled carelessly.
The food laws, the first of the clean and unclean chapters, grounded in the command to be holy because the LORD is holy.
The Day of Atonement, the book's center, with the high priest behind the veil and the scapegoat carrying sin away.
The law of blood, including the verse that explains why blood makes atonement: the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Holiness in ordinary life, from harvest to courtroom, including the command to love your neighbor as yourself.
The Sabbath year and the Jubilee, when debts, slaves, and land are released, grounded in God's ownership of the land.
The covenant's blessings and curses, ending with the promise that God will remember his covenant even in exile.

parts.body:
Leviticus is the third book of the Bible. It has 27 chapters. Almost all of it is God speaking: instructions given to Moses at Mount Sinai, for a people who now have God living in a tent in the middle of their camp.

Many readers who set out to read the Bible from the beginning stall here. Genesis and Exodus are stories. Leviticus reads like a manual. It tells how to bring an offering, what a priest must do, which animals may be eaten, and what to do about a skin disease or mildew in a wall. It can seem far from any life a modern person lives.

It helps to know the one question the whole book answers. Exodus ended with the tent built and the glory of God filling it, so that even Moses could not go in (Exodus 40:35). How can a holy God live among a people who are not holy, and the people live? Leviticus is God's own answer. He gives offerings, priests, a way to become clean again, one day each year when everything is made clean, and a pattern for the whole of life.

The book's best-known words show where it is heading. “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (19:2). Sixteen verses later comes this: ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ (19:18). Jesus named that line as the second of the two commandments on which all the Law and the Prophets hang (Matthew 22:39-40). The book that is hardest to enter holds one of the sentences he set highest.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Leviticus is the middle book of the five books of Moses, which Jews call the Torah. Its Hebrew name is Vayikra, which means ‘and he called’, from its first word. Early Jewish tradition also called it Torat Kohanim, the instruction of the priests.

The story so far runs like this. In Genesis, the first humans were driven from God's presence in Eden, and God chose Abraham's family to bring good to the world. In Exodus, God rescued that family, now a people, from slavery in Egypt. At Mount Sinai he made a covenant with them. They broke it almost at once with a golden calf, and God forgave them. Then they built the tent he had told them to build, the tabernacle, so that he could live among them. “So the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year” (Exodus 40:17). The cloud of God's glory covered it, and “Moses was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting because the cloud had settled on it” (Exodus 40:35).

Leviticus begins at that very moment. “Then the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting” (1:1). God speaks from inside the tent to the man who cannot come in, and he begins to explain how people may come near.

The whole book happens in one place, at the foot of Mount Sinai, and it covers little time. The next book opens “On the first day of the second month of the second year” (Numbers 1:1), so Leviticus fills about one month. Nobody travels anywhere. There are only two short stretches of story: the first days of the priests (chapters 8 to 10) and the case of a man who cursed God's name (24:10-23). Everything else is instruction.

The order matters. These laws come after the rescue, not before it. God says, “I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt so that I would be your God; therefore be holy, because I am holy” (11:45). Israel is not told to keep these laws in order to be rescued. It is told how to live with the God who has already rescued it and now lives next door.

After Leviticus, the book of Numbers takes the ordered camp out into the wilderness toward Canaan, and Deuteronomy gives Moses' last words on the edge of the land.

God had said of the tent, “they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8). Leviticus takes that promise with full seriousness. God is truly there, in the middle of the camp. That is Israel's greatest gift. It is also a danger, because God is holy and the people are not. On the very first day the priests begin their work, two of them die for coming near God in a way he had not commanded (10:1-2).

So the book's question is practical. How can this nearness last? Its answer is that God himself provides the way. The offerings are his gift: of the blood on the altar he says, ‘I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls’ (17:11). The priests are his appointment. The washings and waiting times are his teaching. Nothing in the book is a scheme invented by Israel to win God over.

This sets Leviticus apart from the worship of the nations around Israel. Every nation offered sacrifices and kept priests, and Israel's words for its offerings are close to words found in ritual texts from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast. Egyptian temples served the statues of their gods with daily meals and washings. But in Leviticus there is no image of God in the tent, and God does not need to be fed. A psalm has him ask, “Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Psalm 50:13). There is no rite to control him, and the sacrifice of children, known among Israel's neighbors, is forbidden outright (18:21).

The goal of it all is stated near the end of the book: “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (26:12). The verb for walking is the one used of God walking in the garden in Genesis 3:8. Leviticus is about how a people who have been outside can live near God again.

Leviticus names no author. It presents nearly everything in it as words the LORD spoke to Moses, and sometimes to Moses and Aaron together, at Sinai. Its last verse reads, “These are the commandments that the LORD gave to Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai” (27:34). Jewish and Christian tradition has counted it among the five books of Moses. When Jesus sent a healed man to the priest, he told him to ‘present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing’ (Mark 1:44), which is the law of Leviticus 14. Many conservative scholars, Gordon Wenham among them, hold that the substance of the book goes back to Moses and the wilderness years, whatever later editing it received.

Since the nineteenth century most critical scholars have assigned Leviticus to a priestly source, one of the strands they find woven through the first five books. They treat chapters 17 to 26 as a collection of its own, called the Holiness Code after its refrain about being holy as the LORD is holy. The German scholar Julius Wellhausen placed the priestly writing in or after the exile in Babylon, in the sixth or fifth century BC. Others, among them Yehezkel Kaufmann and Jacob Milgrom, argued that the priestly laws are largely older than the exile. They pointed out that the laws assume a camp in the wilderness and a tent that can be carried, not the temple in Jerusalem. Even a book written down late can preserve much older practice.

Readers across these views agree that Leviticus holds the ritual knowledge of Israel's priests, guarded and handed down with great care. Christians who confess the Bible as God's word hold more than one of these views. These notes do not settle the question.

The book has six parts, and it helps to know which one a chapter belongs to.

Chapters 1 to 7 describe the offerings. There are five kinds, and they are described twice: first for the person who brings them, then for the priests who handle them.

Chapters 8 to 10 tell how the priests began. Moses ordains Aaron and his sons over seven days. On the eighth day they offer their first sacrifices, God's glory appears, and fire from God burns up the offering. Then two of Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, die for offering fire God had not commanded.

Chapters 11 to 15 teach the difference between clean and unclean: food, childbirth, skin disease and mildew, and bodily discharges, each with its way back to being clean.

Chapter 16 is the Day of Atonement. Once a year the high priest goes behind the curtain into the innermost room, and a goat carries the people's sins away into the wilderness. It stands at the center of the book.

Chapters 17 to 26 carry holiness out of the tent and into the whole of life: blood, sex and family, the love of neighbor and of the foreigner, justice in court and market, the priests' own conduct, the feasts of the year, the Sabbath year and the Jubilee, and the blessings and curses of the covenant.

Chapter 27 closes the book with vows and things dedicated to God.

The first half of the book is mostly about how to come near to God. The second half is mostly about how to live as people who are near him. Some phrases come back again and again. Many sections open with the words ‘Speak to the Israelites and tell them’ (1:2), a reminder that most of the book is for the whole people, not only the priests. And in the second half one short sentence closes law after law: ‘I am the LORD’. The laws rest on who God is.

The Hebrew word for an offering is qorban, something brought near. To bring an offering was to come near to God.

An animal offering followed a common pattern, and it should be described plainly. The worshiper brought an animal from his own herd or flock to the entrance of the tent. He laid his hand on its head and killed it himself. The priest then took the blood to the altar and burned the parts that belonged to God. It was costly, physical, and sober. Worship was not something to watch.

There were five kinds. The burnt offering (chapter 1) was burned whole on the altar, a gift with nothing held back; it was offered for the whole nation every morning and evening. The grain offering (chapter 2) was flour, oil and frankincense, the fruit of a person's work. The peace offering (chapter 3) was the one sacrifice the worshiper ate: part was burned, part went to the priests, and the family feasted on the rest before God, in thanksgiving or to keep a vow. The sin offering (chapter 4), which many scholars call the purification offering, dealt with wrongs done without meaning to and with some kinds of uncleanness. The guilt offering (chapters 5 and 6) was for wrongs that did damage: the offender repaid what he had taken, added a fifth, and brought a ram.

The system made room for the poor. Someone who could not afford a lamb could bring two birds, and someone who could not afford birds could bring flour (5:7, 11). When Mary and Joseph came to the temple after the birth of Jesus, they brought the birds (Luke 2:24).

Why blood? The book's own explanation is short: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar” (17:11). Blood stands for life. Life belongs to God. And God gives it back to his people as the means of atonement. Readers have understood the laying on of the hand in several ways: as a sign that the animal stands in the worshiper's place, as a sign that the gift is truly his, or both. The sin offering ends again and again with the same promise: “the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven” (4:31).

Many modern readers find animal sacrifice hard to read about, and that is understandable. It helps to see what Leviticus does not say. It does not say God was hungry, or that his favor could be bought. Israel's prophets said plainly that sacrifice offered without justice and a humble heart was worth nothing: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). The prophets did not reject the altar. They refused to let Israel separate it from the way people treated one another, and Leviticus refuses that too.

parts.h: The priests, and Nadab and Abihu
parts.body:
Aaron, the brother of Moses, and Aaron's sons were set apart as Israel's priests. They offered the sacrifices, but that was not their whole work. They were to “distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean” and to ‘teach the Israelites all the statutes’ (10:10-11). They examined skin diseases, judged hard cases, and blessed the people.

Leviticus never pretends that priests were sinless. Aaron was the man who had made the golden calf. His ordination begins with a sin offering for himself, and his first act as priest is to offer a calf for his own sin (9:8). The letter to the Hebrews draws out the kindness in this. Such a priest “is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is beset by weakness” (Hebrews 5:2).

The story of the priests' first days holds the book's hardest moment. On the eighth day everything goes as God commanded. “Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering” (9:24), and the people shouted for joy. Then, in the next verses, Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu ‘offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command’. “So fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them, and they died in the presence of the LORD” (10:1-2).

The text gives only that one explanation. Readers since ancient times have tried to say more exactly what the fault was: fire taken from the wrong place, going further into the tent than they were allowed, serving after drinking wine (a rule about wine follows in 10:9), or pride. The chapter leaves it open. What it does say is that they came near to God on terms of their own.

Readers are right to find this hard. Two things in the text should be noticed. Such judgments are rare in the Bible, and they come at beginnings, when a pattern is being set. They are not presented as God's usual way with his people, whose ordinary failures the offerings were given to cover. And the book does not make the grief small. Aaron is silent. The whole house of Israel is told that it ‘may mourn on account of the fire that the LORD has ignited’ (10:6). The note on chapter 10 says more.

Leviticus uses four words that a new reader must learn, because the book does not use them the way everyday English does. The priests are told, “You must distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean” (10:10).

Holy means set apart for God and belonging to him. God himself is holy: he is utterly distinct, and he is morally pure. Things, places, days and people become holy when they are given over to him. Common is simply everything else, the stuff of ordinary life. Common is not a bad word.

Clean and unclean are about being fit to come near the holy place. They are not about dirt, and they do not mean good and bad. A clean person could come to the sanctuary. An unclean person had to wait, wash, and in some cases bring an offering first.

Unclean is not the same as sinful. This is the most important thing to know before reading chapters 11 to 15. A woman who had just given birth was unclean (chapter 12), though a child was a gift from God. A husband and wife were unclean until evening after they slept together (15:18). A person who buried a parent was unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11). None of these people had done anything wrong. Uncleanness came from ordinary and often good parts of life. It was temporary, and it ended with time and washing. What was wrong was to ignore it and carry it into the holy place (15:31).

Why these things and not others? The book gives no list of reasons, and readers have offered several. Some, like the medieval Jewish scholar Maimonides, pointed to health, though the Bible never gives that reason. The anthropologist Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), argued that the laws taught wholeness and order: clean animals are the ones that fit their kind completely. Jacob Milgrom and Gordon Wenham noted that most sources of uncleanness are linked with death: a corpse, the loss of blood or seed that carries life, skin that looks like a dying body. The tent was the dwelling of the living God, and the signs of death were kept away from it. These are best taken as partial views of one conviction: Israel's whole bodily life was lived in the presence of a holy God.

The Old Testament also speaks of a second kind of defilement, which is moral. Grave sins such as idolatry, murder and the sexual sins of chapter 18 are said to defile the sinner and the land itself (18:24-25). The scholar Jonathan Klawans set out how the two kinds differ. Ritual uncleanness passes by touch, is temporary, and is not sinful. Moral defilement does not pass by touch, is not washed away with water, and is removed only by atonement or punishment. Keeping the two apart guards a reader from an old mistake, the idea that Leviticus calls a sick person, a new mother or a bleeding woman a sinner. It does not.

So no one should use this book to call another person dirty, and no one should hear it calling them dirty. A word for anyone who has been made to feel unclean, by an illness, by your body or by your past. That is not what this book says of you. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: Atonement, and the Day of Atonement
parts.body:
The verb ‘to make atonement’ runs through the whole book. The Hebrew is kipper. Its exact sense is debated. Some link it with covering, some with wiping clean, and some with a ransom, a payment that spares a life. In Leviticus it seems to carry more than one of these at once, because sin does two things: it puts the sinner in danger, and it leaves a stain that must be cleansed.

Atonement in Leviticus is also wider than the forgiveness of guilt. It is made for a mother after childbirth and for a person healed of skin disease, where no wrong has been done, and even for the altar and the tent. The distance between a holy God and his people is not only a matter of wrongdoing. It also comes from living in a world marked by decay and death, and God himself acts to overcome both.

Once a year the whole system was made new. On the tenth day of the seventh month the high priest took off his splendid robes and dressed in plain linen. He offered a bull for his own sins and those of his household. Then, behind a cloud of incense, he went through the curtain into the Most Holy Place, the innermost room, where the ark stood. It was the only day of the year on which anyone entered it. He sprinkled blood on and before the ark's gold cover, which English Bibles call the mercy seat, first for himself and then, with the blood of a goat, for the people.

Then came a second goat. “Then he is to lay both hands on the head of the live goat and confess over it all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (16:21). The goat was led out and released: “The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place” (16:22). Blood was carried inward to cleanse the sanctuary, and sin was carried outward, away from the people. The Hebrew says that the goat was ‘for Azazel’, a word whose meaning is uncertain: the goat that goes away (the source of the English word scapegoat), a rugged place in the desert, or the name of a wilderness spirit. On every reading nothing is offered to anyone but the LORD, and the goat's task is to take the confessed sins away.

The people had their own part. They were to fast and do no work, “because on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (16:30).

This day is not only a page in an old book. It is Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish year, and Jewish communities keep it still. After the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70 the sacrifices ceased, and Jews kept the day through prayer, fasting and confession. The synagogue service still recites the high priest's service. Jewish teaching has long insisted that the rite never worked apart from a changed heart: the Mishnah says that repentance atones together with the day, and that a wrong done to a neighbor must first be put right with the neighbor. Christians should speak of this living observance with respect.

Christians also read the day in the light of Jesus, because the New Testament draws the line itself. Hebrews says that Christ ‘entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood’ (Hebrews 9:12), and that the yearly repeating of the sacrifices showed that they pointed beyond themselves (Hebrews 10:1-4). Jews and Christians both read Leviticus as a book about drawing near to the holy God. They differ over where, since AD 70, the way into his presence is found.

From chapter 17 on, the book turns from the tent to the town. Holiness is no longer only a matter for priests at the altar. It reaches the field, the family, the court and the shop. “You are to be holy to Me because I, the LORD, am holy, and I have set you apart from the nations to be My own” (20:26).

Chapter 19 is the heart of it, and many readers think it the heart of the book. It moves through ordinary life with one command after another. Leave the edges of your field for the poor and the foreigner (19:9-10). Pay a worker his wages the same day (19:13). “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind” (19:14). Judge fairly, favoring neither the poor nor the rich (19:15). Do not spread slander (19:16). Use honest scales (19:36). And in the middle of these stands the sentence Jesus set beside the love of God: “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (19:18).

In that verse the neighbor is a fellow Israelite. So the chapter goes on to say the same thing of the outsider: “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (19:34). The reason given is memory. Israel knew what it was to be a stranger. Jewish teachers treated this command as central. Hillel, a generation before Jesus, summed up the law by saying that a person should not do to a neighbor what he himself hates, and Rabbi Akiva in the early second century called the love of neighbor a great principle of the Torah.

These chapters also hold some of the hardest pages in the Bible, and the chapter notes face them one by one. Chapter 18 forbids incest, adultery and the sacrifice of children to Molech, a rite in which children were killed. Chapter 20 attaches penalties, including death, to many of the same acts. Those penalties were the law of ancient Israel as a nation under God, decided by courts and witnesses. Christians have generally held that they belonged to Israel's civil law and are not carried into the church, and they are no pattern for anyone to take up today.

Two verses in these chapters, 18:22 and 20:13, speak of a man lying with a man as with a woman. Christians read them in more than one way. The chapter notes set out the readings in the words of those who hold them and take no side, as the site's notes on Romans 1 and 1 Corinthians 6 do. One thing is plain on any reading: nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person, and no one may use these verses to harm or shame anyone.

Chapter 21 bars a priest with a physical defect from serving at the altar, though he still eats the holy food. That rule concerned one office in one sanctuary. It is not a statement of any person's worth before God. Every person, with any disability or illness, is made by God and is precious to him.

parts.h: Feasts, the Jubilee, and the covenant
parts.body:
The last chapters make time and land holy as well.

Chapter 23 sets out the year. Every seventh day is a Sabbath. In spring come Passover and the week of Unleavened Bread, then the offering of the first sheaf of the harvest, and seven weeks later the Feast of Weeks. In the seventh month come a day of trumpet blasts, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived for a week in shelters made of branches to remember the wilderness. God calls them ‘My appointed feasts’ (23:2). They are his appointments with his people. Jewish communities keep these feasts today. Christians differ on whether to keep them: most churches hold that they were fulfilled in Christ and leave such days to conscience (Colossians 2:16-17; Romans 14:5-6), while some believers keep them gladly. Easter and Pentecost grew from this calendar.

Chapter 25 gives rest to the land. Every seventh year the fields were to lie unsown. After seven times seven years came the fiftieth year: “you are to consecrate the fiftieth year and proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants. It shall be your Jubilee” (25:10). Land that a family had been forced to sell went back to it, and Israelites who had sold themselves into service went free. The reason was that neither land nor people finally belonged to those who held them. “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine” (25:23). Whether the Jubilee was ever regularly kept is uncertain; the Old Testament has no clear record of one. But it shaped Israel's hope.

The same chapter holds a hard passage. Israelites were not to be held as slaves, but verses 44 to 46 allowed slaves bought from other nations to be held for life. That is in the text, and it cannot be explained away. These notes do not defend slavery. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used texts like these to defend slavery as biblical. That was a misuse of Scripture, and it was wrong. The note on chapter 25 faces the passage at more length.

Chapter 26 sets out the covenant's blessings and curses: rain and peace if Israel keeps faith, and disaster and exile if it will not. These words were spoken to a nation living in its land under the covenant of Sinai. They describe the long direction of its life together. They are never God's verdict on any one person's illness or loss. When the disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). And the chapter does not end in ruin. Even in exile, God says, “I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them; for I am the LORD their God” (26:44).

Chapter 27 ends the book with vows, the promises people made to give something to God, and how such gifts could be bought back.

parts.h: How Christians relate to these laws
parts.body:
Christians do not offer animals, and most do not keep the food laws. Yet the church has always read Leviticus as Christian Scripture. How do those two things fit? Christians answer in more than one way.

The New Testament itself holds two things together. Jesus said, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). Paul wrote that “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12). Yet Mark comments on the teaching of Jesus, “(Thus all foods are clean.)” (Mark 7:19). Peter was told in a vision, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). And Hebrews calls the law ‘only a shadow of the good things to come’ (Hebrews 10:1). Every Christian tradition has had to explain how these belong together.

The most widely used account divides the law of Moses into three kinds. It is found in Thomas Aquinas, in John Calvin, and in the Westminster Confession of 1646. Moral laws, such as the Ten Commandments and the love of neighbor, express God's own character and still bind. Ceremonial laws, such as the sacrifices, the food laws and the feasts, were fulfilled in Christ and are no longer practiced. Civil laws governed Israel as a nation and ended with that nation, though the justice in them still teaches. On this account most of Leviticus 1 to 16 is ceremonial, and chapter 19 holds much that is moral.

Lutherans stress the difference between law and gospel. The law commands and shows sin; the gospel gives and forgives.

Dispensational readers, and those who hold what is called New Covenant Theology, say that the covenant of Sinai as a whole ended with Christ. Believers now live under ‘the law of Christ’ (Galatians 6:2), which takes up much of the moral law in a new form. On this account a command of Leviticus binds a Christian where the New Testament repeats it, as it repeats the love of neighbor.

A small movement called theonomy has argued that Israel's civil laws, penalties included, should still guide governments. Most Reformed churches have rejected that view.

Some Christians keep parts of these laws by choice. Seventh-day Adventists avoid the meats that chapter 11 calls unclean. Many Jewish believers in Jesus keep the food laws and the feasts as part of their Jewish life. Paul asked believers who differ over food and days not to judge one another (Romans 14:3-6).

Jewish tradition reads the book differently again. For Jews these commands are given to the Jewish people as a gift to be studied and loved. Many of them could be kept only while the temple stood. The food laws and the feasts still shape Jewish life.

These notes take no side among the Christian accounts. All of them agree on some things. Leviticus is God's word. Christians do not offer its sacrifices, because Christ ‘offered for all time one sacrifice for sins’ (Hebrews 10:12). Its call to holiness is repeated to the church: “Be holy, because I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16). And its command to love one's neighbor stands at the center of the Christian life: “Love does no wrong to its neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10). Of any law in the book a reader can ask what it showed Israel about God's holiness and his care for people, even where the law is no longer kept as written.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Leviticus
parts.body:
The New Testament reads Leviticus more closely than almost any other book of the Old Testament, and it draws its own lines from the book to Jesus.

The letter to the Hebrews draws the longest. It reads the tabernacle as ‘a copy and shadow of what is in heaven’ (Hebrews 8:5), the high priest as a picture of Christ, and the Day of Atonement as a picture of his death. “He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). The sin offering burned outside the camp is set beside the place where Jesus died: “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).

Paul uses the book's words too. He says that God presented Christ ‘as the atoning sacrifice’ (Romans 3:25). The Greek word there is the one the old Greek translation of Leviticus used for the mercy seat, the cover of the ark. He writes that Christ ‘gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God’ (Ephesians 5:2), the language of the pleasing aroma of the burnt offering. Peter says that believers were redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

The Gospels show Jesus among people Leviticus calls unclean. He touched a man with a skin disease (Mark 1:41). A woman who had bled for twelve years touched his cloak (Mark 5:27). He took a dead girl by the hand (Mark 5:41). In each case the uncleanness did not pass to him; health and life passed from him. And he still sent the healed man to the priest with the offering Leviticus required (Mark 1:44). He did not treat the law with contempt.

The command to love one's neighbor is quoted by Jesus, by Paul and by James (Mark 12:31; Galatians 5:14; James 2:8). The promise of chapter 26, that God would walk among his people, is quoted by Paul of the church (2 Corinthians 6:16), and the last pages of the Bible see it kept at last: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3).

These lines do not make Israel's worship empty. As the site's notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real. It has the true shape of the thing that casts it, and God truly met his people at this tent and forgave them there, as the book itself promises. One thing must be said plainly. For centuries some Christians used the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews and for Jewish worship. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.

parts.h: How Jews and Christians have read it
parts.body:
Leviticus is Israel's Scripture first, and it has shaped Jewish life more than almost any other book. Its food laws became a place where loyalty to God was tested. Around 167 BC the king Antiochus IV tried to stamp out Jewish practice in Judea, and the books of Maccabees tell of Jews who died sooner than eat pork. When the temple fell in AD 70, Judaism had to live without an altar. A well-known rabbinic story tells of Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai comforting a disciple at the ruins by pointing to Hosea 6:6: deeds of loving-kindness now make atonement. Prayer, the study of Torah and acts of kindness took the place of the altar in Jewish life. The afternoon prayer is still called Minchah, after the grain offering.

Christians have read the book in their own ways. The church remembers Mary's purification and the presentation of Jesus in the temple, the rite of Leviticus 12, on the second of February, forty days after Christmas. Many churches kept a service of thanksgiving for a mother after childbirth. The words of Leviticus 25:10 about proclaiming liberty were cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia. In the nineteenth century, defenders of slavery in the United States quoted the same chapter, while those who fought slavery appealed to the image of God in every person, to the exodus and to the New Testament. The same book was read for freedom and misused against it, and the misuse must be named honestly.

In modern study two names stand out. Mary Douglas, an anthropologist, taught many readers to look for order and meaning in the food laws. Jacob Milgrom wrote a commentary in three volumes (1991 to 2001) that remains the standard work; he read the whole system as a way of teaching Israel to choose life.

A new reader may find Leviticus strange for a long time. That is no failure. It was written for people who lived with God in the middle of their camp and had to learn, day by day and with their bodies, that he is holy and that he wanted them near. Read slowly, it asks a question that does not go out of date: what would it mean for the whole of a life, its meals and money and family and time, to belong to God?

hard.line: Why would God ask for animals to be killed and burned? What sacrifice meant in Leviticus, and what it did not mean.
Nadab and Abihu die for offering unauthorized fire. What the text says, what it leaves open, and the grief it does not hide.
The food laws: why some animals were unclean, and how Mark 7 and Acts 10 bear on Christians.
A mother is unclean after childbirth, and longer after a daughter. Uncleanness is not sin and not shame.
A person with a skin disease lives outside the camp. What the disease was, and what the chapter never says of the sick.
Bodily discharges and uncleanness: a status, not a verdict on any body or any woman.
The goat ‘for Azazel’: the main readings of an uncertain word.
How could a goat carry sins away? The Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur today, and how Hebrews reads it.
The life is in the blood: the ban on eating blood, and how Christians have understood it.
Child sacrifice to Molech, forbidden outright.
‘As with a woman’: the readings Christians hold, set out in their own terms. No one may use this verse to harm or shame any person.
The death penalties of chapter 20, stated soberly, and never as a pattern for today.
A priest with a physical defect may not serve at the altar. What the rule was, and why it says nothing of anyone's worth before God.
A man is put to death for cursing the Name, and ‘eye for eye’ as a limit on courts.
Slaves from other nations held for life: the passage faced honestly, with its misuse named.
The covenant curses: a warning to a nation, never God's verdict on one person's illness or loss.
Why are people given different values in silver? What the figures measured, and what they did not.

words.line: ‘And he called’, the Hebrew name of the book, from its first word (1:1).
An offering, from the Hebrew verb ‘to come near’. To bring an offering was to draw near to God (1:2).
The burnt offering, from the verb ‘to go up’. The whole gift went up to God in smoke (1:3-9).
The peace offering, related to shalom, peace or well-being. The one sacrifice the worshiper ate (3:1; 7:11-18).
The sin offering, which many scholars call the purification offering. It dealt with wrongs done without meaning to and with some uncleanness (4:1-35).
The guilt offering, for wrongs that did damage. It came with repayment and a fifth added (5:14-6:7).
To make atonement. The word has been linked with covering, with wiping clean and with a ransom that spares a life (4:20; 16:30).
The gold cover of the ark, called the mercy seat in English Bibles, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (16:14).
Hebrew qadosh: set apart for God and belonging to him. God is holy, and he calls his people to be holy (11:44; 19:2).
Hebrew tame: not fit, for a time, to come near the holy place. A ritual state, not dirt and not the same as sin (chapters 11 to 15).
Hebrew taher, to be clean: fit to come near. The priest's word ‘clean’ brought a person back into the full life of the people (13:17; 14:20).
The skin disease of chapters 13 and 14, once translated leprosy. It covers several conditions, and even mildew in cloth and walls.
The word for where the second goat was sent (16:8). Its meaning is uncertain; older Bibles give ‘scapegoat’.
The foreigner living among Israel, without land or family there. Israel is told to love him as itself (19:33-34).
The ram's horn, and so the Jubilee, the fiftieth year announced by its blast (25:9-10).
To redeem: to buy back a relative's land or freedom, the duty of the nearest of kin (25:25, 48-49).

timeline.what: Ritual texts from Ebla in Syria describe a goat driven out into the wasteland in a rite of cleansing, an early parallel to the goat of chapter 16.
Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast name offerings with words close to the Hebrew ones.

timeline.when: The first month of the second year
timeline.what: The tabernacle is set up at Sinai on the first day of the month, a year after Israel left Egypt (Exodus 40:17), and the LORD calls to Moses from it (1:1).

timeline.when: Seven days, and the eighth day
timeline.what: Aaron and his sons are ordained (chapter 8). On the eighth day the glory of the LORD appears and fire burns up the offering (9:23-24). Nadab and Abihu die (10:1-2).
All the words of Leviticus are given at Sinai before the first day of the second month, when Numbers begins (Numbers 1:1).
The Gezer tablet, a small limestone tablet found in 1908, lists the farming months of the year in an order like that of the feasts.
Two small silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem carry a form of the priests' blessing of Numbers 6.
Jerusalem falls to Babylon and Judah goes into exile. 2 Chronicles 36:21 says the land then enjoyed its Sabbaths, echoing 26:34-35.
Ezekiel, a priest in exile, draws on the language of Leviticus and restates its rules for priests in his vision of a new temple (Ezekiel 44).
The prophet Malachi rebukes priests who offer blind and lame animals, which Leviticus 22 forbids (Malachi 1:8).
Antiochus IV tries to suppress Jewish practice in Judea. The books of Maccabees tell of Jews who die sooner than eat pork.
The Romans destroy the temple in Jerusalem. The sacrifices cease, and Jews keep the Day of Atonement through prayer, fasting and confession.
The Mishnah is compiled. A whole tractate, Yoma, tells how the Day of Atonement was kept in the temple.
William Tyndale coins the English word ‘scapegoat’ for the goat of chapter 16.
A Norwegian physician identifies the bacterium of the disease now called leprosy. Its marks are not those of the skin disease in Leviticus 13.
August Klostermann gives chapters 17 to 26 the name the Holiness Code.
Mary Douglas publishes Purity and Danger, reading the food laws as teaching wholeness and order.
Jacob Milgrom's three-volume commentary on Leviticus appears. It remains the standard work.

places.name: Goshen, in Egypt
places.line: Leviticus looks back to ‘the land of Egypt, where you used to live’ (18:3). Israel had lived in Goshen, usually placed in the eastern Nile delta; it is drawn here roughly.

places.name: Canaan
places.line: The land ahead: ‘the land of Canaan, into which I am bringing you’ (18:3). Many laws in the book look forward to life there. Drawn roughly.

teaching.mapNote: Leviticus names almost no places. Every word of it is given at Mount Sinai, and where that mountain lay is debated, so it is not drawn. The map shows only the two lands the book itself names: Egypt, which Israel had left, and Canaan, which it had not yet reached. Both are drawn roughly.
